The morning light filtered through the heavy curtains, casting long shadows across the wooden floor. Elena stirred beneath the thick woolen blanket, reluctant to leave the warmth of her bed. Outside, the city was already awake—the sound of carriage wheels on cobblestones drifted up from the street below, mingled with the distant cry of a newspaper vendor.

She had been dreaming again. The same dream that had visited her every night for the past week: a vast library with shelves that stretched endlessly upward, filled with books whose pages were blank. She wandered through the aisles, searching for a single word written on any page, but found only silence and empty paper.

When she finally opened her eyes, the dream dissolved like mist, leaving only a vague unease. She sat up slowly, pushing the blanket aside, and reached for the glass of water on the nightstand. It was warm—the servant must have brought it hours ago.

The room was modest but comfortable. A writing desk sat beneath the window, covered in papers and ink bottles. Her journal lay open, the last entry dated three days ago. She had not written since then. The words, when they came, came slowly, as if each one had to be dragged from some deep and reluctant well.

Breakfast was served in the small dining room on the ground floor. Her uncle was already at the table, hidden behind the morning edition of the Herald. He did not look up when she entered, but she heard him fold the newspaper slightly, the way he always did when he was listening but pretending not to.

Good morning, Uncle, she said, taking her usual seat. The porridge was too hot, the tea too weak. She ate without tasting, her mind still half-lost in the library of her dreams.
